name: JFrog
tagline: Universal artifact repository manager for DevOps pipelines.
description: JFrog holds built binaries in a universal artifact repository, moves them through release stages, and scans them for vulnerabilities.
pros: This repository's GitLab review treats JFrog Artifactory as the dedicated artifact manager that general-purpose package registries trail in depth.
Binaries of different package types — Docker images, npm packages, Maven artifacts — sit in one store instead of one server per format.
Scanning runs against artifacts that are already stored, so findings surface before promotion rather than after deployment.
Promotion advances a built artifact through environments instead of rebuilding it at each stage.
Build and deploy scripts talk to the repository over ordinary HTTP endpoints for upload, download, and metadata lookups.
cons: Our dataset lists JFrog's pricing model as Paid, so no free tier is recorded here and evaluation begins with a paid conversation.
Adding JFrog to a multi-tool stack adds a user directory, an authentication surface, and more webhooks — the overhead this repository's GitLab review describes.
Pricing is recorded inconsistently in this repository, as a $75-149/mo band here against an enterprise-tier treatment in the stack guide, so budgeting needs vendor confirmation.

features.name: Universal artifact storage
features.description: Binaries in several package formats are held in one repository that both build and deploy steps can query.

features.name: Multiple package formats
features.description: Container images, language packages, and generic release files are served from the same installation rather than separate servers.

features.name: Release promotion paths
features.description: An artifact built once can be advanced through environments without being rebuilt, so what was tested is what ships.

features.name: Artifact vulnerability scanning
features.description: Stored binaries are checked for known vulnerabilities before they move to the next stage of a release.

features.name: Build integration endpoints
features.description: Pipeline steps upload artifacts, download them, and read metadata through standard HTTP calls.

features.name: Storage retention policies
features.description: Rules decide how long superseded binaries remain on disk, which is what keeps a long-lived repository from filling indefinitely.

features.name: Artifact permissions
features.description: Repository-level permissions decide who may read from, write to, or delete stored binaries.

features.name: Metadata search across binaries
features.description: Stored artifacts can be located by package, version, or build information instead of by browsing directory trees.

content.title: What JFrog is for
content.body: JFrog's central product, Artifactory, is a universal artifact repository: one store that build jobs upload to, deployments download from, and release steps query for metadata along the way. This page's dataset describes it as a universal artifact repository manager for DevOps pipelines and records a 4.1/5 rating from 620 reviews. It is not a CI system and not a container registry alone; it is the layer where built artifacts live between the pipeline that produced them and the environments that consume them.

content.title: One repository, many package formats
content.body: The word universal in that descriptor refers to format coverage. Instead of standing up a separate server for each package type, build and deploy steps point at one repository. The formats and consumers that matter in a typical release pipeline, described generically rather than as a vendor checklist, are these:
items: Container images: builds push images to a hosted registry and deploys pull the same artifact later.
Language packages: npm, Maven, NuGet, and similar client libraries are served to build agents from the same store.
Generic binaries: release archives, installers, and firmware files that no language registry claims.
Deployment inputs: charts and configuration consumed by the release step rather than by a developer's editor.
Metadata: version, build, and scan information attached to each stored artifact so a deployment traces back to the pipeline that produced it.

content.title: Moving a binary through release stages
content.body: Promotion is the workflow that separates an artifact repository from a bucket. A build produces one artifact, that artifact is verified, and then the same bytes are advanced toward production instead of being rebuilt at each step, so what ran in staging is what ships. Teams model this either as repositories per stage or as paths and properties on a single store, with permissions that allow promotion but not edits. Because the artifact does not change between stages, promotion also shortens a release: the deploy step downloads something that already exists.

content.title: Scanning what is already stored
content.body: An artifact repository is the last place a binary passes before deployment, which is why scanning belongs there. Vulnerability checks run against stored artifacts and their metadata, so a dependency published after a build can still be flagged before that version moves onward. JFrog's scanning capability is documented by the vendor as a companion to Artifactory, though this repository records no packaging or bundling details — buyers should confirm what is included at the tier they are quoted rather than assume it here.

content.title: Pricing recorded on this page
content.body: Our dataset marks JFrog as a Paid product with a list price band of $75-149/mo, and no free tier is recorded, so the first conversation with the vendor is a paid one. The same repository holds a conflicting signal: its developer-tools stack guide treats Artifactory as an enterprise-tier line item and recommends that smaller teams use a bundled registry instead. Both entries were written at different times for different purposes and neither should be quoted as current. Nothing on this page comes from operating JFrog; it is drawn from repository records and vendor-published material, so confirm pricing with the vendor before budgeting.

content.title: Standing in this repository's records
content.body: JFrog appears in twenty comparison files stored with this review and wins one of them, the SourceForge record. It is scored below CircleCI at 4.3, Grafana at 4.5, Postman at 4.6, and Datadog at 4.6, though those products do different jobs and the score is a weak guide to fit. On this site's CI/CD ranking JFrog sits eighth of eight entries, which reads as a category mismatch rather than a verdict on artifact storage: prose on that same page treats JFrog as the specialist that bundled registries are measured against.

content.title: Fit, and what this repository does not say
content.body: Evidence for JFrog in this repository is thinner than for most neighboring pages: outside the comparison files, substantive prose about it appears only in the GitLab review and in the developer-tools stack guide, so this closing section stays short rather than padded. What it does support: teams with mature pipelines that need binaries stored, scanned, and promoted across environments, at a budget consistent with an enterprise-tier purchase. It fits less well for a small team that only needs somewhere to push images, where the stack guide's advice to use the code host's bundled registry applies directly.

faqs.question: What does JFrog replace in a toolchain?
faqs.answer: The separate per-format package stores. This repository's GitLab review frames JFrog Artifactory as the dedicated artifact manager that a bundled package registry imitates without matching in performance or depth.

faqs.question: Is there a free tier in JFrog?
faqs.answer: Our dataset lists JFrog's pricing model as Paid with a $75-149/mo band and no free tier recorded. Another file here treats Artifactory as an enterprise-tier item, so confirm current plans with the vendor.

faqs.question: Why scan artifacts that were already scanned in CI?
faqs.answer: Scanning stored binaries catches vulnerabilities disclosed after a build was produced, and it holds at the point where a version is promoted rather than only where it was compiled.

faqs.question: How does JFrog score in this dataset's comparisons?
faqs.answer: JFrog holds 4.1/5 from 620 reviews here and wins one of the twenty head-to-head records stored against it, the SourceForge comparison; most others go to products in adjacent categories.

faqs.question: Which teams is JFrog aimed at?
faqs.answer: The stack guide in this repository treats Artifactory as an enterprise-tier purchase and advises smaller teams toward a bundled registry instead, which indicates the buyer size it expects.

author: Marcus Rivera
learningCurve: Upload and download are simple; repository layout, promotion rules, and scan policy take real practice
whoShouldUse: Engineering organizations with mature pipelines that need binaries stored, scanned, and promoted across environments at an enterprise-tier budget.
whoShouldNotUse: Small teams that only need somewhere to push container images; this repository's stack guide advises using the code host's bundled registry below enterprise scale.
